categories.name: Evidence of impact
categories.intro: Does the product actually improve learning, and how do they know?

categories.name: Data privacy
categories.intro: What happens to student and staff data, during the contract and after it ends?

questions.question: What specific student outcome did your research measure, and how was it measured?
questions.why_it_matters: "Improves learning" can mean test scores, engagement, time on the platform, or teacher satisfaction. Only some of those are learning.
questions.weak_answer: Usage numbers, engagement rates, or satisfaction surveys presented as if they were learning gains.

questions.question: Who funded the research, and who conducted it?
questions.why_it_matters: Company-funded studies aren't automatically wrong, but they need more scrutiny, and you deserve to know who paid.
questions.weak_answer: "Independent researchers" with no names, or a study run entirely by the company's own team without saying so.

questions.question: Did the study compare students who used the product with similar students who didn't? How were they chosen?
questions.why_it_matters: Without a comparison group, gains could come from normal growth, a new teacher, or anything else that happened that year.
questions.weak_answer: Pre/post results with no comparison, or comparisons where schools chose for themselves whether to participate.

questions.question: How large was the effect, and for which students?
questions.why_it_matters: A result can be statistically significant and still too small to matter, or it may hold only for one group of students.
questions.weak_answer: "Statistically significant" with no effect size, or results reported only for the highest-using students.

questions.question: Which version of the product was studied, and how different is it from what we would buy today?
questions.why_it_matters: AI products change quickly, including the models underneath them. Evidence about last year's version may not describe this year's.
questions.weak_answer: A study of an older version or a different underlying model, presented as evidence for the current product.

questions.question: When you say the product is "research-based," do you mean research on this product, or research on the ideas behind it?
questions.why_it_matters: Citing general learning science (like retrieval practice) is not evidence that this particular product works.
questions.weak_answer: A list of well-known learning science studies, none of which tested the product itself.

questions.question: Has the evidence been reviewed or published outside your company? If you claim an ESSA evidence tier, who determined it?
questions.why_it_matters: Vendors often assign their own evidence tier. Outside review and a clear source for the claim make it far more credible.
questions.weak_answer: A white paper hosted only on the company website, or an ESSA tier the company assigned to itself.

questions.question: What results have you found that were neutral or negative?
questions.why_it_matters: Studies that find no effect are often never shared. A vendor who discusses them is giving you a more complete picture.
questions.weak_answer: "None." Every product has some setting, group, or measure where it didn't help.

questions.question: How much use did students need to see results, and how often did schools actually reach that level?
questions.why_it_matters: If results require 90 minutes a week and most schools average 20, the evidence may not apply to how you'd really use it.
questions.weak_answer: Results reported only for students who met the recommended usage, with no information on how many did.

questions.question: How is the AI's output checked for accuracy before students or teachers rely on it, and what is its known error rate?
questions.why_it_matters: AI tools can produce confident, wrong content. You need to know how often that happens and who catches it.
questions.weak_answer: "Our model is highly accurate" with no error rate, testing process, or description of human review.

questions.question: What student and staff data do you collect, and what is each type used for?
questions.why_it_matters: You can't judge risk without a specific list. Collecting more than the product needs increases exposure.
questions.weak_answer: "Only what's necessary" without an actual list of data fields and purposes.

questions.question: Is any of our data used to train or improve AI models, yours or a third party's?
questions.why_it_matters: Data used for training can be hard or impossible to remove later. This should be an explicit yes or no in the contract.
questions.weak_answer: "De-identified data may be used to improve our services," with no detail on what that includes.

questions.question: Which outside companies, including AI model providers, receive our data, and under what terms?
questions.why_it_matters: Many AI tools send data to another company's model. Your data is only as protected as the weakest company it passes through.
questions.weak_answer: "Trusted partners" with no names, or no mention of the model provider at all.

questions.question: How long do you keep our data, and how is it deleted when the contract ends?
questions.why_it_matters: Data kept indefinitely is a long-term risk. You want a timeline and written confirmation of deletion.
questions.weak_answer: No retention timeline, or deletion only "upon request" with no confirmation.

questions.question: Will you sign our state or district student data privacy agreement?
questions.why_it_matters: Many states and districts use standard agreements, often through the Student Data Privacy Consortium. Willingness to sign one is a basic signal.
questions.weak_answer: Only the company's own terms of service, or a refusal to negotiate any changes.

questions.question: How does the product handle students under 13, and what consent does it rely on?
questions.why_it_matters: Federal law (COPPA) sets rules for collecting data from children under 13. Ask your district's legal or privacy staff how it applies to you.
questions.weak_answer: An assumption that the school has handled consent, with no explanation of what the product collects from young students.

questions.question: What happens to our data if your company is acquired, merges, or shuts down?
questions.why_it_matters: Edtech companies are bought and closed often. The contract should say what happens to your data when that happens.
questions.weak_answer: Not addressed in the contract, or "we'd handle that at the time."
